replies.author: FjorgVanDerPlorg
replies.body:
People are asking about the artwork. They can't see the code, or anything the code does and therefore don't care about the coding part at all, which is coincidentally the only part you explain. You wanna show off code, you have to show what it does.

2/3d models and artwork is what that comparison before/after image shows and what people are asking about/the comments about your "prompting" are referring to.

Are there any 3d models in that scene, or is it all just gen AI images?

Either way you have a problem with the characters in the April image, they are fully lit characters in a dark night time scene. You are gonna need to tint their materials at a minimum to make them conform to the scene lighting. This isn't an exclusively AI problem, people made these mistakes with marketplace assets before AI, but AI has definitely exploded the rate at which people are seeing it.

I assume that scene is just some 2d sprites on a 2d image, generated with GPT or Midjourney. When it comes to 2d AI generative stuff, you typically have to do a LOT of extra work to keep the art style consistent and that includes lighting. This is the part people are calling slop. The acid test is does the character feel like they are in the scene, or painted on a layer on top of it. Because fully lit characters in a dark scene has some big uncanny valley problems that comes with it, in an art style that shouldn't be having uncanny valley issues.

replies.author: FjorgVanDerPlorg
replies.body:
I think you miss the point, I never said it was about realism, I said it was about consistent art style. The "Uncanny Valley" comparison was about the fact I can look at that image and just know the lighting on the models is wrong.

The problem is with the material/texture on the 3d model then, because just looking at them, they are too well lit for that scene. I dev in other game engines, mostly UE5 so I don't know exactly how this is done in unity, but in UE5 I often see this problem - ie where it still looks too well lit despite being backlit to intentionally try and make it conform with the scene light levels. Often it comes down to the 3d modeller using an emissive output in the material graph/shader.

Or it could just be ambient/environment light too strong. If your global ambient/skylight intensity/GI is set high enough to "fill" the scene for gameplay readability, it'll flatten shadows on the models and make them pop against a dark background. The background image won't be affected by this the same way the 3D models are.

Or indirect lighting or light probes baked in a brighter environment. If the light probes/reflection captures were baked when the scene was lighter or outdoors, models will sample incorrect ambient bounce lighting.

Or the compositing approach itself. Since you're separating the stage into layers and the background is a generated/photoshopped image rather than actual 3D geo, the models can't receive occlusion or bounce light from it. The scene looks dark because the image is dark, but the models are lit by actual Unity lights that may not match the painted-in atmosphere.

This is an easy to read problem as well, average TA will spot it right away.

The fix isn't necessarily complex - reduce ambient/fill light aggressively, lean harder into the rim-only lighting for moonlit scenes, and don't be afraid to let the models go quite dark. Players read silhouette and motion more than surface detail anyway at that camera distance/angle/light levels.
